t: LeetCode 3179 – Find the N-th Value After K Seconds
o: Each second replaces the array with its prefix sums. Watching a[n-1]: after 1 second it is C(n, n-1)... concretely for n = 4 the last column reads 1, 4, 10, 20, 35, 56 for k = 0..5 — these are binomial coefficients C(k + n - 1, n - 1). Indeed applying the prefix-sum operator k times to the all-ones vector yields binomial coefficients (stars and bars). So the answer is C(n + k - 1, n - 1) mod 1e9+7. With n, k ≤ 1000 even the direct O(n·k) simulation passes, but the closed form is O(n + k).
k: Prefix-sum applied k times to all-ones gives binomial coefficients: answer = C(n + k - 1, n - 1).
Modular inverses via Fermat's little theorem since 1e9+7 is prime.

a.i: Compute factorials up to n + k - 1 and evaluate C(n + k - 1, k) · ... i.e. fact[n+k-1] · inv(fact[k]) · inv(fact[n-1]) modulo 1e9+7.
s: Precompute factorials mod p up to n + k.
Return fact[n+k-1] * inverse(fact[k]) * inverse(fact[n-1]) mod p.
a.t: O(n + k) for factorials plus O(log p) for modular inverses
a.sp: O(n + k) for the factorial table

a.i: Faithfully apply the process: k rounds of in-place prefix sums. With n, k ≤ 1000 this is at most 10^6 additions.
s: Repeat k times: for i from 1 to n-1 set a[i] = (a[i] + a[i-1]) mod p.
a.t: O(n · k) — at most 10^6 operations under the given constraints

w: Lead with the simulation (safe, obvious), then impress with the binomial closed form — derive it by spotting the pattern in small cases or via generating functions. Pitfall: taking the modulus only at the end overflows in fixed-width languages; reduce every addition. Follow-up: value of a different index j (answer becomes C(k + j, j)), or huge n, k where only the formula survives.
